idiom_name: Object#extend with role modules (per-object singleton class); SimpleDelegator for wrapping roles
implementation_notes: Ruby performs the pattern's dynamic attachment natively: obj.extend(Borrower) adds a role module to that object's singleton class, so the role exists on exactly one subject, and define_singleton_method covers one-off role methods, with respond_to?/is_a? playing the part of hasRole. When a role must wrap and forward the whole core interface instead of being mixed in, DelegateClass/SimpleDelegator generate the forwarding and can even re-point at another delegate at runtime. The explicit role-object structure is still warranted when role state must be persisted or audited separately from the core, or when a uniform add/get/remove protocol must be exposed to other subsystems.
code_sketch:
module Borrower                        # role module: mixed into one customer only
  def borrow(amount) = "#{name} borrows #{amount}"
end

class Customer
  def initialize(name) = (@name = name; @roles = {})
  def add_role(mod) = (@roles[mod.name] ||= extend(mod))     # enters the singleton class
  def get_role(mod) = (@roles[mod.name] if singleton_class.include?(mod))
end

customer = Customer.new("Ann").add_role(Borrower)            # role lives on this instance only
customer.borrow(500)
pitfalls: A module cannot be un-extended: removing a role means rebuilding the object (or undefining singleton methods), and refinements cannot be extended at all (TypeError).
dup does not copy the singleton class while clone does, so role sets silently disappear through one copy path and survive the other.
Module instance variables live on the extended object, so role state shares one namespace with core state and can collide with it.
